svg.text: The 2016 Sterling Flash Crash (GBP/USD, 7 October 2016)
Down ~6% in two minutes, then mostly back -- no headline, just an empty market.
GBP/USD, deep in the Asian session
Quiet, thin overnight market
~6% in ~2 min to a 31-year low ~1.18
then mostly recovered, minutes later
BIS report: no single cause
1. Time of day -- the thinnest,
least-liquid hour of the day.
2. Options-hedging: real demand
to sell pounds.
3. Stop-loss execution triggering
a cascade of market sell orders.
4. Algorithms selling into a market
with almost no one on the other side.
A modest imbalance met no resistance.
Where you have seen each piece before
Thin liquidity is the flip side of the spread (Ch1 L4): fewer participants, so price moves further per order.
The stop cascade is the stop-out mechanism (Ch3 L2) at market scale: stops trigger stops trigger stops.
The timing is the calendar discipline (Ch2 L4) in reverse: the market was fragile because almost no one traded.
A stop held through the plunge filled far below its level -- then price recovered. Right on direction, wrecked on execution.
Execution and liquidity are real risks, not background detail. Trade liquid hours; size for a thin-market spike.
Source: BIS Markets Committee report on the 7 October 2016 sterling flash event.
